text:
R. c. Anderson

2013 QCCS 3565

JC 1961

SUPERIOR COURT

(Criminal Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No.:

500-01-044931-100

DATE:

July 17
th
,
2013

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:

THE HONOURABLE

CAROL COHEN, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

v.

BARRINGTON ANDERSON

______________________________________________________________________

TRANSCRIPTION AND REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

on sentence

(rendered orally on March 1
st
, 2013)

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Barrington Anderson was charged with two counts
of robbery and two counts of possession of an imitation firearm, relating to
two separate bank robberies which occurred five days apart, on March 12
th

and March 17
th
, 2010, as appears from the indictment:

Count 1 ‑ Possession
of imitation firearm on March 12
th
, 2010: “On or about
March 12, 2010, in Montréal, district of Montréal, did use an imitation
firearm while committing an indictable offence of robbery contrary to

section 85 (2)
a) (3) of the
Criminal Code
.”

Count 2 ‑ Robbery
at the TD Bank, March 12
th
, 2010: “On or about
March 12, 2010, in Montréal, district of Montréal, did rob employees and
clients of TD Bank, contrary to
section 344(1)
b) of the
Criminal
Code
.”

Count 3 ‑ Possession
of imitation firearm on March 17
th
, 2010: “On or about
March 17, 2010, in Montréal, district of Montréal, did use an imitation firearm
while committing an indictable offence of robbery, contrary to

section 85 (2)
a) (3) of the
Criminal Code
.”

Count 4 ‑ Robbery
at the Laurentian Bank, March 17
th
, 2010: “On or about
March 17, 2010, in Montréal, district of Montréal, did rob employees and
clients of Laurentian Bank, contrary to
section 344(1)
b) of the
Criminal
Code
.”

[
2
]

On February 6
th
, 2013, after a trial
before judge and jury which began on January 7
th
, 2013, Mr.
Anderson was acquitted on the two counts relating to the first robbery on March
12
th
, 2010, and found guilty on the two counts of robbery and use of
an imitation firearm relating to the March 17
th
, 2010 robbery at the
Laurentian Bank.

[
3
]

The Court heard representations on sentence on
February 27
th
, 2013, and will now render a judgment on sentence on
the two counts relating to the Laurentian Bank robbery.

[
4
]

Mr. Anderson was 29 years old at the time of the
robbery and is now 32 years old. He is not married, but has 5 children (aged
14, 13, 9, 7 and 5), none of whom were in his custody at the time of his arrest
or at the time of the March 17
th
robbery, and he found out about the
existence of his eldest child only recently. He did not offer any evidence with
respect to sentencing and did not file any letters of support from family
members or friends.

[
5
]

As appears from Exhibit S-1, the only exhibit
filed for the purpose of sentencing, Mr. Anderson has several previous
convictions which will be detailed below, including a previous conviction for
robbery.

[
6
]

As at the present date, March 1
st
,
2013, Mr. Anderson has been detained preventatively for exactly 2 and one-half
years (30 months), as he was arrested on August 30
th
, 2010.

Facts

[
7
]

The Court will summarize the pertinent facts
with respect to the Laurentian Bank robbery before proceeding to consider the
principles applicable to sentencing, keeping in mind the provisions of
section
724 (2)
(
a
) of the
Criminal Code
(“Cr. C.”), namely that
all facts, express or implied, that are essential to the jury's verdict of
guilty should be accepted as proven for the purpose of sentencing.

[
8
]

At around 3 pm
[1]

on March 17
th
, 2010, a bank robbery occurred at the Laurentian Bank
on Darlington road near Van Horne.

[
9
]

Mr. Anderson, the robber, first entered the
vestibule of the bank and stopped at the ATM machine, as if he was going to
carry out a transaction at the machine. As appears from the cameras in the
vestibule, Mr. Anderson took out a bank card but he did not insert the card
into the ATM machine, although he has an account at the Laurentian Bank. In
fact, the bank records for his account in March 2010, produced at trial, show
no transactions on that day in Mr. Anderson’s Laurentian Bank account.

[
10
]

As appears from the pictures captured by the
camera at the ATM machine, Mr. Anderson was wearing a dark hood, dark
clothing and a yellow bandana around his neck, and was carrying sunglasses in
one hand. After a few seconds, Mr. Anderson put on the sunglasses and pulled up
the yellow bandana over his mouth and nose. He was not wearing gloves.

[
11
]

Mr. Anderson then entered the main hall of the
bank carrying a black bag. Upon entering the bank, he was captured by several
video cameras and his actions were seen by bank employees who testified at
trial.

[
12
]

The video cameras inside the bank showed Mr.
Anderson waving a black gun in one hand and pointing it at the tellers, and he
tossed the bag over the counter.

[
13
]

The director of customer service at the
Laurentian Bank at the time (Annick), who actually worked at another branch but
was working at the Darlington branch that day, testified that Mr. Anderson, on
entering the bank, said “
Give me the money
” in English, and then tossed
his bag over the counter.

[
14
]

When he realized that the money was being placed
in a bank bag and not into his own bag, Mr. Anderson jumped over the counter,
placing his palm on the countertop. At trial, a palm print on that part of the
countertop was identified as being Mr. Anderson’s.

[
15
]

Mr. Anderson then told the employees to transfer
the money from their bag to his bag. As they were doing so, he went to a cash
drawer behind the counter and took cheques and money. Once the transfer into
his own bag was completed, he said he didn’t have enough money and pointed his
gun at the employees again.

[
16
]

According to Annick, Mr. Anderson then went to
jump back over the counter, dropping a blue cellular phone from his pocket. He
picked up the phone, jumped over the counter and went towards the exit,
lowering the bandana from his face.

[
17
]

When asked in cross examination which hand he
used when jumping over the counter, Annick testified that she was looking down
because she was too scared. When asked if the gun was touching the counter, she
answered that she couldn’t say, with the stress of having a gun so close to
her. She said that the gun looked like a police gun, black and 6 or 8 inches
long.

[
18
]

As appears from the video images, when Mr.
Anderson saw a female client at a far teller, he put his bandana back up over
his face, went back to the counter and took money and/or cheques from the
customer. Once he had done so, Mr. Anderson turned and said not to follow him
because if they did, he would shoot them. Annick testified that he spoke and
acted in an aggressive manner.

[
19
]

Annick no longer works for the Laurentian Bank,
but now works in a foster home. She testified that she knew the robbery lasted
only a few minutes (in fact, Mr. Anderson was inside the bank for 90
seconds), but said that it felt very long in her head.

[
20
]

Nassina, a teller at the time, testified that
the robber, Mr. Anderson, came into the bank calling “
Give me money, I want
money
” in English. As soon as he came in, he threw his bag over the
counter. He was pointing to the left and to the right with his gun and wearing
a hood, a balaclava, a coloured scarf or bandana covering his face, and
sunglasses. She testified that at one point, he jumped over the counter onto “
our
side
”, and that he was limber and very agile.

[
21
]

According to Nassina, when he saw there was not
enough money, the robber shouted “
Give me more
”. When asked what he was
saying when he was holding the gun, Nassina said “
I don’t remember, I was
very, very scared. I was frozen
”. She said she could also see the fear in
the eyes of her colleagues, adding that “
we were not expecting that
”.

[
22
]

Nassina testified that the robber was yelling
and nervous. When he left, she testified that the robber “
stared at us,
pointing with his gun, saying not to follow him

or he would shoot us
”.
She testified that it was a shock for her, she was very affected and resigned
immediately afterwards from the bank. She is now a teacher.

[
23
]

Sarra, who at that time was head of customer
services at the Laurentian Bank, Darlington branch, testified that the robber,
Mr. Anderson, came into the bank wearing a hood, black jacket, and a bandana
covering his face. He was armed. He told them to stand up, put their hands up and
asked them to give him money. He wanted the money in his own bag, according to
Sarra, and repeated this loudly, but one teller didn’t understand as she had
not seen his bag, which he had thrown over the counter.

[
24
]

Sarra testified that the robber then jumped over
the counter to get the money into his bag. When the transfer of money into his
bag was made, the robber said –“
That’s all? I want more
”.

[
25
]

According to Sarra, the robber then jumped back
to the other side, crying out not to follow. She testified that he did a U-turn
and went to take money from a customer at the counter, and then he left, saying
not to follow him. Sarra is no longer an employee of the bank and is now a
student.

[
26
]

Sarra and another bank employee testified that
cheques, which had been deposited on March 17
th
, 2010, by customers
(including the customer at the far counter), were later brought back to the
bank by another customer, who had received them in the mail. It was established
at trial that Mr. Anderson’s fingerprints were found on some of those cheques,
and these fingerprints led to Mr. Anderson’s arrest in August 2010.

[
27
]

Mr. Anderson admitted that his fingerprints were
on the cheques in question. However, in his testimony at trial, he denied
taking the cheques from the bank. Instead, he testified that he had found these
cheques and others in an abandoned apartment, and that he had mailed the
cheques to a name and address appearing on them, although without postage. He
also testified that he had brought other cheques to Jewish organizations,
including an organization known as the Mada Centre.

[
28
]

A rabbi from the Mada Centre testified at trial
that a “
male black person
” did bring cheques to his organization in
2010, although he could not identify Mr. Anderson as being that person. The
cheques delivered to the Mada Centre were never returned to the bank or to
police.

[
29
]

Given the verdicts with respect to the
Laurentian Bank robbery, it is clear that the jury did not accept Mr.
Anderson’s testimony that his fingerprints appeared on cheques stolen from the
bank only because he had found them in an abandoned apartment. The verdict
indicates that the jury believes that Mr. Anderson’s fingerprints, which
appeared on the cheques, along with his palm print on the counter of the bank,
were there because he was the robber on the video, who took the cheques from
the cash drawer and from the customer at the far counter, and who jumped over
the countertop.

[
30
]

As noted above, Mr. Anderson did not testify at
the sentencing hearing, nor was any proof offered with the exception of Exhibit
S-1, the list of his previous convictions, produced by the Crown.

[
31
]

Exhibit S-1 can be summarized as follows.

[
32
]

In 1996, as a juvenile, Mr. Anderson was
convicted of two counts of robbery (“
vol avec violence
”, s. 343 (
a
) Cr. C.)
and received a sentence of 15 months, with 9 months probation.

[
33
]

In 1998, as an adult, Mr. Anderson was convicted
of two counts of armed robbery (“
vol qualifié
”, s. 344 (
b
) Cr. C.)
and received a sentence of 15 months, with two years of probation.

[
34
]

In 1999, Mr. Anderson was convicted of two
counts of assault (s. 266 (
a
) Cr. C.) and one count
of conjugal violence (more specifically, sequestration ‑ section
279 (2) (
a
) Cr. C.), and he received a one month
sentence for each count, consecutive to the sentence he was serving at the
time, along with 3 years of probation.

[
35
]

In 1999, Mr. Anderson was convicted of failure
to respect his probation, and received a 14 day sentence.

[
36
]

In 2003, Mr. Anderson was convicted of theft of
less than $5,000, and he received a fine of $400 and one year of probation.

[
37
]

In 2008, Mr. Anderson was convicted of threats
and criminal harassment (two counts, section 264 Cr. C.), and
received a suspended sentence and two years of probation.

[
38
]

Finally, on July 13
th
, 2009, Mr.
Anderson pleaded guilty to the offence of possession and carrying a concealed
weapon, and received a total sentence of six months, as he was sentenced on the
same day to breach of probation, for which he received a sentence of three
months, less a day.

[
39
]

Mr. Anderson was no longer on probation at the
time of the Laurentian Bank robbery on March 17
th
, 2010.

[
40
]

Mr. Anderson testified in his defense at trial.
He noted that he was born in Côte-des-Neiges and moved several times with his
family (mother, father and several siblings). He completed primary school and
high school.

[
41
]

Mr. Anderson also testified that he was and is
very close with his paternal grandmother, who used to live on Darlington near
the Laurentian Bank, and who is 97 years old. He worked at various jobs
(including with Publisac, in woodworking and renovations, as an apprentice
mechanic and for some community organizations) and played sports, especially
football in Verdun and LaSalle, until he suffered a shoulder injury in the fall
of 2009.

[
42
]

He also testified that he was very active musically,
that he was encouraged to do shows and recordings when he was around 16 or 17
years old. He registered a music company a few years ago, an enterprise which
gave him income and some royalties, including selling compilation CDs. He has
done local radio, promoting his music, and participated in reggae festivals.

[
43
]

At the time of the robbery, Mr. Anderson was
living with a girlfriend, Ms. Davis, who had a child (although this child is
not his). As noted above, he has 5 children, one of whom he only learned about
recently. He testified that he has a good relationship with his other children
and saw them often when he was not in jail.

[
44
]

In 2010, Mr. Anderson was on social assistance
and was also working as a car mechanic and doing renovations. He testified that
he gave money to support his children, but did not testify as to how much money
he was giving them. As noted, none of the mothers of these children testified.

The principles of sentencing

[
45
]

The fundamental purpose and principles of
sentencing are set out at sections 718 and following of the
Criminal Code
,
in particular at
section 718
Cr. C., which underlines that the
purpose of sentencing is to contribute, along with crime prevention
initiatives, to respect for the law and a just, peaceful and safe society by imposing
just sanctions having specific objectives:

718. The
fundamental purpose of sentencing is to contribute, along with crime prevention
initiatives, to respect for the law and the maintenance of a just, peaceful and
safe society by imposing just sanctions that have one or more of the following
objectives:

(
a
) to
denounce unlawful conduct;

(
b
) to
deter the offender and other persons from committing offences;

(
c
) to
separate offenders from society, where necessary;

(
d
) to
assist in rehabilitating offenders;

(
e
) to
provide reparations for harm done to victims or to the community; and

(
f
) to
promote a sense of responsibility in offenders, and acknowledgment of the harm
done to victims and to the community.

[
46
]

Section 718.1 Cr. C. stipulates that a
sentence must be proportionate both to the gravity of the offence and to the
degree of responsibility of the offender.

[
47
]

Section 718.2 Cr. C. sets out some, but not
all, of the aggravating and mitigating factors which should be taken into
account in determining the appropriate sentence:

718.2. A court that imposes a
sentence shall also take into consideration the following principles:

(
a
) a
sentence should be increased or reduced to account for any relevant aggravating
or mitigating circumstances relating to the offence or the offender, and,
without limiting the generality of the foregoing,

(i) evidence
that the offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on race,
national or ethnic origin, language, colour, religion, sex, age, mental or
physical disability, sexual orientation, or any other similar factor,

[…]

(iii.1) evidence
that the offence had a significant impact on the victim, considering their age
and other personal circumstances, including their health and financial
situation,

[…]

[…]

shall
be deemed to be aggravating circumstances;

(
b
) a
sentence should be similar to sentences imposed on similar offenders for
similar offences committed in similar circumstances;

(
c
) where
consecutive sentences are imposed, the combined sentence should not be unduly
long or harsh;

(
d
) an
offender should not be deprived of liberty, if less restrictive sanctions may
be appropriate in the circumstances; and

(
e
) all
available sanctions other than imprisonment that are reasonable in the
circumstances should be considered for all offenders, with particular attention
to the circumstances of aboriginal offenders.

[
48
]

Section 725 Cr. C. instructs a sentencing
judge to consider, if it is possible and appropriate to do so, any other
offences of which the offender was found guilty by the same court, and to
determine the sentence to be imposed for each offence. Furthermore, the Court
may consider any facts forming part of the circumstances of the offence that
could constitute the basis for a separate charge, according to subsection 725 (1) (
c
)
Cr. C.:

725. (1) In determining the
sentence, a court

(
a
) shall
consider, if it is possible and appropriate to do so, any other offences of
which the offender was found guilty by the same court, and shall determine the
sentence to be imposed for each of those offences;

[…]

(
c
) may
consider any facts forming part of the circumstances of the offence that could
constitute the basis for a separate charge.

[
49
]

In the present case, pursuant to
subsection
344 (1)
(
b
) Cr. C., the charge of robbery carries a
maximum of life imprisonment, and no minimum, as a firearm was not used in the
commission of the offence (an
imitation
firearm does not trigger the
minimum sentences provided for at
subsection 344 (1)
(
a
):

344. (1) Every
person who commits robbery is guilty of an indictable offence and liable

(
a
) if
a restricted firearm or prohibited firearm is used in the commission of the
offence or if any firearm is used in the commission of the offence […]

(
b
) in any other case, to imprisonment for life.

[
50
]

As for the charge of use of an imitation firearm
in the commission of the indictable offence of robbery
(subsection 85 (1) (
a
) Cr. C.), this carries a
minimum penalty of one year for a first offence and a maximum penalty of
fourteen years (subsection 85 (3) (
a
) Cr. C.),
which is to be served
consecutively
to any other punishment arising from
the same events, pursuant to subsection 85 (4) Cr. C.:

85. (2) - Every person commits an
offence who uses an imitation firearm

(
a
) while
committing an indictable offence,

[…]

whether or
not the person causes or means to cause bodily harm to any person as a result
of using the imitation firearm.

85. (3) - Every person who
commits an offence under subsection (1) or (2) is guilty of an indictable
offence and liable

(
a
) in the case of a first offence, except as provided in paragraph
(b), to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years and to a minimum
punishment of imprisonment for a term of one year; and

[…]

85. (4) - A sentence imposed on a
person for an offence under subsection (1) or (2) shall be served consecutively
to any other punishment imposed on the person for an offence arising out of the
same event or series of events and to any other sentence to which the person is
subject at the time the sentence is imposed on the person for an offence under
subsection (1) or (2).

[
51
]

Given
subsection 85 (4) Cr. C., both parties agree that the
sentence for the offence of use of an imitation firearm, a minimum of one year,
must be served
consecutively
to the sentence on the offence of robbery,
subject of course to the conditions of section 718.2 (
c
) Cr. C.,
namely that the combined sentence should not be unduly long or harsh.

[
52
]

Finally, on the issue of preventative detention,
the Court must consider subsection 719 (3) Cr.

C. as
recently amended, which instructs the sentencing judge to impose a 1:1 ratio
for every accused detained since February 22
nd
, 2010 (and therefore
to Mr. Anderson, who was arrested on August 30
th
, 2010), although
article 719 (3.1) provides an exception to that rule, as appears from
the following provisions:

719. (1) A sentence
commences when it is imposed, except where a relevant enactment otherwise
provides.

(2) Any time during which a
convicted person is unlawfully at large or is lawfully at large on interim
release granted pursuant to any provision of this Act does not count as part of
any term of imprisonment imposed on the person.

(3) In determining the
sentence to be imposed on a person convicted of an offence, a court may take
into account any time spent in custody by the person as a result of the offence
but
the court shall limit any credit for that time to a maximum of one day
for each day spent in custody
.

(3.1) Despite subsection (3),
if
the circumstances justify it, the maximum is one and one-half days for each day
spent in custody
unless the reason for detaining the person in custody was
stated in the record under subsection 515(9.1) or the person was detained
in custody under subsection 524(4) or (8).

(3.2)
The court shall give
reasons for any credit granted
and shall cause those reasons to be stated
in the record.

(emphasis added)

Submissions by the parties

[
53
]

The Crown has asked for a global sentence of
seven years of imprisonment, more specifically six years on the count of
robbery and one year consecutive on the count of use of an imitation firearm,
with credit for preventative detention of 30 months in a ratio of 1:1 days for
each day of pre-trial detention, as provided for at subsection
719 (3) Cr. C.

[
54
]

The attorney for the Crown has outlined many
aggravating factors, which will be reviewed below, and maintains that there are
few if any mitigating factors. As for the preventative detention, the Crown
argues that the circumstances do not justify a credit of more than one day for
each day which Mr. Anderson spent in custody.

[
55
]

The defense has suggested a sentence of two
years on the count of robbery and one year consecutive on the count of use of
an imitation firearm, for a total of three years (36 months), with credit for
preventative detention in a ratio of 1.5 days for each day of pre-trial
detention, and therefore with a credit of 45 months (30 x 1.5), requiring his
immediate release.

[
56
]

M
e
Kennedy, attorney for the
defense, submits that there are many mitigating factors, including the fact
that Mr. Anderson is black (subsection 718.2 (
a
) (i) Cr. C.),
that he has five children and that he comes from an underprivileged background.
As for pre-trial detention, the defense attorney submits that her client has
been detained at Rivière‑des‑Prairies under “
nasty conditions
”,
although no testimony or evidence was offered with respect to this allegation.
She furthermore submits that there were delays in the proceedings which would
militate in favour of a credit for pre-trial detention higher than the ratio of
1:1.

Discussion

[
57
]

The Court acknowledges the many aggravating
factors in this case with respect to the robbery in the Laurentian Bank, as
submitted by the Crown. These aggravating factors include the significant
impact the robbery had on the victims working in the bank on that day (subsection
718.2 (
a
) (iii.1) Cr. C.) and the fact that there
could have been other distinct charges resulting from the facts of this
robbery, including use of a disguise, pointing a firearm at the tellers and
uttering threats, pursuant to subsection 725 (
c
) Cr. C,
cited above.

[
58
]

The aggravating factors can be summarized as
follows:

•

objective gravity of the offence of robbery,
with a possibility of life imprisonment;

•

the use of a disguise in the robbery, making it
an aggravating factor pursuant to section 725 Cr. C., as use of
a disguise is a distinct offence (section 351 (2) Cr. C.);

•

the impact of the robbery on the victims, namely
the bank employees - the employees of the bank who testified at trial suffered
significant trauma, and all have ceased working in a bank;

•

the fact that Mr. Anderson pointed his firearm
at tellers, and even held the gun near an employee’s head, another distinct
offence pursuant to subsection 87 (1) Cr. C., whether the
firearm is loaded or not;

•

the fact that the robbery was a premeditated and
planned robbery of a financial institution, as appears from the disguise, the
use of the gun, his actions at the ATM machine (where he pretended to be doing
a transaction), bringing a bag which he threw over the counter. In other words,
as argued by the Crown, this robbery was not carried out on a whim;

•

the fact that Mr. Anderson uttered threats,
including death threats, to the employees, telling them they should not follow
him or he would shoot or kill them, another offence pursuant to
section 264.1 Cr. C., an offence for which, moreover, he had
already been convicted in the past;

•

the fact that it was a bank robbery using a
firearm rather than a note (a hold-up), which is considered to be at the higher
and more serious end of the spectrum or range of robberies;

•

Mr. Anderson’s previous criminal record,
including convictions for theft, robbery, possession of a concealed weapon and
violent offences, such as assault -  two counts - and conjugal sequestration.

[
59
]

As for mitigating factors, there are few, if
any. Despite the arguments raised by Mr. Anderson’s attorney, there was no
evidence whatsoever offered that the offence was in any way related to the fact
that Mr. Anderson is black, despite subsection 718.2 (
a
) (i) Cr. C.,
and the Court will not take this into account.

[
60
]

Furthermore, while Mr. Anderson does have five
children, he has not testified as to an economic difficulty relating to their
support or indeed, as to what support he was or is giving to them. He has not
produced any letters or testimony indicating the impact his continued
incarceration would have on his family, although he testified as to several
sources of income prior to his arrest, including public assistance.

[
61
]

Mr. Anderson has not expressed any remorse,
including with respect to the stress imposed upon the bank employees during and
following the robberies, as appeared from their testimony. Moreover, he has not
offered evidence with respect to his prospects for rehabilitation, which would
be a mitigating factor, especially given his previous convictions. Finally, he
has not offered any evidence with respect to community support.

[
62
]

In fact, the only mitigating factor which could
possibly be considered by the Court is the fact that Mr. Anderson returned the
cheques he stole from the bank, bringing some to the Mada Centre, and mailing
others to one customer (albeit without postage so that the customer had to go
to the post office and pay $1.14 in order to retrieve her cheques). This,
according to his testimony at trial, was as a result of the links between
Jamaican Rastafarians and African Jews, in particular that he felt he had
obligations towards Jews and Jewish organizations, and therefore felt he must
return the cheques on which his fingerprints were found. He did testify,
however, that his then-girlfriend Ms. Davis “
was upset at him because
he mailed those cheques
”, telling him he should throw them into the
garbage, as “
other people
” had also told him to do. On the other hand,
while some stolen cheques were indeed returned, none of the cash stolen from
the bank was ever recovered.

[
63
]

As to Mr. Anderson’s degree of responsibility
(section 718.1 Cr. C.), the evidence shows that Mr. Anderson was
alone during the robbery of March 17
th
, 2010. Nevertheless, his
attorney M
e
Kennedy argued at some length that there are “
elements
in the evidence which would reduce his responsibility
”, including the fact
that he had an unhappy childhood, was bullied and taunted as a child and only
recently discovered that he had another daughter. However, the evidence does
not justify any mitigation. Moreover, although he had broken up with Ms. Davis
at the time of his arrest on August 30
th
, 2010, he conceded in
cross-examination that she called the police the proceeding night, just prior
to his arrest, when he broke into her apartment in the middle of the night. In
sum, there is nothing whatsoever in the evidence which would reduce
Mr. Anderson’s degree of responsibility for the robbery of March 17
th
,
2010.

[
64
]

How does this translate into the appropriate
sentence to be imposed in this case?

[
65
]

Author Clayton C. Ruby, in his book
Sentencing
[2]
, suggests a range of between
two and nine years incarceration for bank robberies in the case of younger men,
namely those in their 20s to 30s, like Mr. Anderson. Ruby adds that sentences
of one to three years are at the lower end and typically apply to the “
threatening
note
” type of robbery (paragraph 23.413), whereas the higher range – four
to nine  years – applies to robberies involving violence or weapons, such as
the present case (paragraph 23.420). In sum, Ruby notes that “
harsh
sentences expressive of general deterrence
” are often seen to be necessary
in cases of bank robbery:

23.404 Bank robbery tends to be
regarded as more serious than robbery of individuals or of small commercial
establishments […] harsh sentences expressive of general deterrence are often
seen as the necessary antidote to the particular temptation held out by the
availability of large amounts of currency.
[3]

[
66
]

The jurisprudence cited by Ruby and by the Crown
shows a similar range of sentences in the case of bank robberies.

[
67
]

In three cases of armed robberies with a
handgun, cited by Ruby at paragraph 23.420, the accused received sentences
of between six and seven years of incarceration.

[
68
]

In
Helpard
[4]
,
a sentence of six years was imposed for a bank robbery using a mask and
handgun; the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal gave weight to protection of the
public and general deterrence in upholding that sentence, despite the youth and
unfortunate upbringing of the perpetrator.

[
69
]

In
Scherle
[5]
, the accused held a gun to
the head of a teller and threatened the lives of two elderly men - he received
a sentence of seven years.

[
70
]

In
Gifford
[6]
, the perpetrator in a bank
robbery used a mask and a loaded handgun and told the customers to get on the
ground and demanded money from the teller; the robber received a total sentence
of 6.5 years.

[
71
]

In the case of
Delage
[7]
, in which it was impossible
to determine whether a real gun or an imitation gun was used in a bank robbery,
as in the present case, the accused had previous convictions, including for
robbery. The Quebec Court of Appeal reduced a sentence of twelve years on bank
robbery to eight years.

[
72
]

In
Nilsson
[8]
,
a 28 year old bank robber initially received two sentences of seven years each
on two counts of bank robbery committed 13 days apart, which the trial judge
decreased to an overall eight year sentence on the “totality principle”. In
that case, the accused had a lengthy criminal record, and there was fear and
stress to the victims of the bank robbery, as here, but there were several
mitigating factors, including his youth, remorse and motivation to complete
high school, a difficult childhood and lack of violence in the robberies. The
court in that case emphasized the principles of deterrence, denunciation and
public safety.

[
73
]

In
Corkum
[9]
,
a 26 year old bank robber, who used a threatening note in broad daylight,
received a sentence of eight years on two bank robberies – the perpetrator had
a criminal record, there was premeditation and there were no mitigating
factors.

[
74
]

In
Nembhard
[10]
, a 34 year old was
convicted of bank robbery, attempted robbery and wearing a mask. He was
sentenced by the trial judge to a total of nine years imprisonment – four years
concurrent for one count of bank robbery and one of attempted bank robbery,
four years each concurrent for use of a disguise on both occasions, two years
consecutive for use of imitation firearm during the attempted robbery, and
three years consecutive for use of imitation firearm during the robbery. There
were no mitigating factors in that case other than a guilty plea, and the
accused had a record which included three previous robberies. The Ontario Court
of Appeal reduced the two concurrent sentences for use of an imitation firearm
– from two to one year for the attempted robbery, and from three to two years
for the robbery, for a total sentence of seven years instead of nine.

[
75
]

In
SA
[11]
,
an accused with a lengthy criminal record was found guilty of four counts of
bank robbery and three counts of use of an imitation firearm. He received a
sentence of four years on each robbery (concurrent) and one year consecutive on
each of two counts of use of imitation firearm, plus an additional 1.5 years on
another count of use of imitation firearm, for a total sentence of 7.5 years
imprisonment. Mitigating factors included his young age (24), presence of
daughter and girlfriend, and potential for rehabilitation.

[
76
]

In
DS
[12]
,
the accused, aged 29, pled guilty to three counts of robbery with notes
presented to tellers, who suffered fear and stress, along with one count of
assault. He had a criminal history since the age of 13, including robbery and
weapons offences, and was addicted to drugs. However, he had no actual weapon
on him during the robberies in question. He received seven years each for three
counts of robbery (concurrent).

[
77
]

In
Thompson
[13]
, a 30 year old with no
criminal record filed a guilty plea with respect to eleven counts of robbery,
including robberies of tellers in financial institutions. The trial judge
sentenced him to eight years, which was reduced to 6.5 years (six years plus
credit of six months for pre-trial detention) by the British Columbia Court of
Appeal, which held that the first judge, in placing emphasis on deterrence and
denunciation, failed to give sufficient weight to the accused’s prospects for
rehabilitation and remorse.

[
78
]

Finally, in
Bezdan
[14]
, a 36 year old with seven
prior robbery convictions filed a guilty plea on one count of bank robbery.
Aggravating factors included trauma to bank tellers, danger to the public and
the fact that he was on probation at the time of the crime, and he had a long
standing addiction to cocaine and heroin. He was sentenced to five years
imprisonment by the trial judge, who emphasized trauma to the tellers and
placed considerable weight on his criminal record. The sentence was upheld by
the British Columbia Court of Appeal.

Deterrence and denunciation

[
79
]

Before proceeding to determine the appropriate
sentence, the Court must consider the appropriate weight to be given to
deterrence and denunciation in the present case, in light of section
718 Cr. C., and remembering that restorative justice is geared
towards reconciliation, which requires introspection, a desire to contemplate
what went wrong, an acknowledgement of the undesirable consequences of one's
actions, an openness to other points of view and a willingness to accept such
points of view as legitimate, in other words, a capacity for self-criticism and
a will to bring about positive changes.

[
80
]

Mr. Anderson has shown no willingness to
acknowledge the undesirable consequences of his actions in this case, nor to
bring about positive changes. He has not expressed remorse, nor has he
acknowledged the undesirable consequences of his actions. As a result,
deterrence becomes especially important here, especially given his previous
convictions for similar offences of theft, robbery, assault and weapons
possession.

[
81
]

In the circumstances, given the aggravating
factors noted above, the Court must impose a sentence which is somewhat harsher
than those in analogous circumstances.

Sentence

[
82
]

Given all of the circumstances discussed above,
given the sections of the
Criminal Code
and the authorities referred to above,
amongst others, the undersigned is of the view that a sentence of five years
incarceration on the count of robbery is warranted.

[
83
]

As for the count of use of an imitation firearm,
the Court accepts the submission of the defense that a sentence of one year
concurrent, the minimum, would be appropriate.

[
84
]

The Court also accepts the submission of the
Crown, that there should be a lifetime ban on the possession of firearms as
well as an order to furnish a DNA sample.

[
85
]

In setting these sentences, the Court takes into
consideration all of the factors discussed above, including the numerous
aggravating factors, the absence of mitigating factors, Mr. Anderson’s previous
record on similar offences, the fact that this was a hold-up with threats of
violence, the planned nature of the offence, the absence of remorse, the
importance of deterrence and denunciation, the protection of the public, and
the fear and trauma experienced by the tellers and bank employees, all of whom
felt obliged to change jobs following the robbery. This global sentence of six
years incarceration is well within the range set out by the doctrine and jurisprudence,
and it is even on the low side, when one considers other analogous situations
described above. The undersigned believes that this sentence is also
proportionate both to the gravity of the offence and to the degree of
responsibility of the offender, Mr. Anderson, who acted alone throughout.

Credit for pre-trial detention

[
86
]

What of the credit Mr. Anderson’s pre-trial
detention of two and a half years? As noted above, the Crown argues that the
credit should be on a 1:1 ratio, whereas the defense submits that the credit
should be 1.5 days for every day of pre-trial detention.

[
87
]

Article 719 (3.1) Cr. C., cited
above, provides an exception to the rule of a 1:1 ratio, provided that it is
justified by the circumstances.

[
88
]

M
e
Kennedy argued that the
conditions of his detention were inappropriate, although no testimony or
evidence was offered with respect to same. She added that Mr. Anderson has not
been able to see his grandmother, who is 97 years old, and may not live too
much longer. She also argued that his detention has prevented Mr. Anderson
from pursuing his musical career.

[
89
]

Finally, M
e
Kennedy submitted
that delays in the proceedings resulted in a longer than usual pre-trial
detention, including a preliminary hearing which took place over a period of 8
months as well as a postponement of the trial from June 2012, which the defense
submits was entirely the result of a change of Crown prosecutor, but which the
Crown alleges was attributable to the defense, noting that before the
appearance of M
e
Kennedy in the file, the defense also changed
attorneys several times.

[
90
]

On this last point, the undersigned cannot
accept the submission that there is any evidence of an unusually long pre-trial
detention resulting from the actions of the Crown or the state.

[
91
]

It is true that the Crown prosecutor changed
during the course of this file, prior to May 2012, however this did not delay
the trial. In fact, it was M
e
Kennedy who, in May 2012,
requested postponement of the trial (scheduled to take place in June 2012)
until January 2013 as she did not feel that enough time was allocated for the
trial, which she believed would take two months and not just one month as had
been allocated.

[
92
]

Moreover, at the beginning of the trial before
the undersigned, in January 2013, M
e
Kennedy made similar
representations to the undersigned, arguing that the case would take closer to
seven weeks and not four as planned, and worrying that the trial could not be
completed within the time set out for the jury at their selection.

[
93
]

In fact, the Crown’s evidence before the
undersigned took only two weeks (from January 10
th
until
January 25
th
, 2013). This was despite the fact that M
e
Kennedy
failed to appear at Court on several occasions without reason – unsubstantiated
headaches or doctors’ appointments, despite requests by the Court to provide
details as to the nature of her ailments and the medication she was taking.
This two week period also included M
e
Kennedy’s consistently
late arrivals at trial and her numerous requests for breaks and suspensions, on
an almost daily basis.

[
94
]

As for the defense evidence before the
undersigned, it took only three days, despite announced witnesses who did not
appear and M
e
Kennedy’s late arrival by more than two and a
half hours on the last day of proof, when the Court and jury were waiting for
her to appear to Court with a witness who she said she was picking up and who
never actually appeared.

[
95
]

Furthermore, despite the postponement of the
trial from 2012, an alibi was presented during Mr. Anderson’s testimony before
the undersigned in 2013 which had never previously been revealed to the Crown
attorneys or to the investigator.

[
96
]

The Court could also find nothing unusual in the
scheduling of the preliminary inquiry in this case, which took place over a
period of eight months.

[
97
]

Finally, it is worth noting that M
e
Kennedy
missed a court date in December 2012 for a preparatory conference, although
this did not delay the trial.

[
98
]

In sum, no evidence was offered to show that
delays which took place prior to trial were unusual, unjustified or that they
occurred despite requests to proceed by the defense, and no such delays were
entirely attributable to the Crown or to the police and state authorities.

[
99
]

As a result, the undersigned will not take into
account any delay in bringing this case to trial, with respect to the
appropriate ratio to be applied concerning pre-trial detention, even if such a
ground could be considered as justifiable circumstances in light of the
jurisprudence discussed below.

[
100
]

The undersigned therefore returns to subsection
719 (1) Cr. C., which provides that the Court “
shall
”
limit any credit for pre-trial detention to a maximum of one day for each day
spent in custody. In fact, subsection 719 (3.1) provides that the Court
may only derogate from this ratio of 1:1 “
if the circumstances justify it
”.

[
101
]

What are these circumstances then, which can
justify such a derogation?

[
102
]

The jurisprudence makes it clear that the
reasons must not be related only to the
length
of time of pre-trial
detention, but rather to the accused’s specific remand conditions, an onus of
proof which is on the defense. Moreover, while the circumstances need not be
exceptional, they must be individual to the accused.

[
103
]

This arises from several recent appeal court
decisions, in particular the cases of
Carvery
[15]
and
Stonefish
[16]
, discussed by the attorneys
during their argument.

[
104
]

In
Stonefish
, an accused had pled guilty
to several counts and received a credit of 1.5 days for every day of pre-trial
detention from the sentencing judge. The Court of Appeal of Manitoba reviewed
all of the applicable legislation and jurisprudence, including the decision in
Carvery
,
and reduced the credit to 1:1, holding that the onus for enhanced credit beyond
1:1 ratio is on the accused and that the circumstances submitted must be particular
to the accused, as appears from the following extracts of the opinion of
Justice Freda Steel:

81. In
summary then, I conclude that a reading of the provision in a holistic manner
leads to the conclusion that
the circumstances justifying enhanced credit
need not be exceptional.  However,
they
do need to be individual to the accused
.
Loss of remission and statutory release may be individual circumstances
justifying enhanced credit where the accused can bring evidence to the court
that, had he or she been a sentenced inmate, they would have most probably
received remission and/or statutory release. […]

[…]

84. This interpretation also accords with the
conclusion of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in
Carvery
(at para.
85
):

In the end,
taking into account the words of ss. 719(3) and (3.1) in their grammatical and
ordinary sense and read in the entire context of the legislative scheme and the
object of the
Act
, the legislation provides for judicial discretion to
grant credit of up to 1.5:1 for time spent in pre-sentence custody if a judge
is satisfied that the circumstances justify it, which includes consideration of
the potential loss for the offender of earned or statutory remission and
parole.  ….

[…]

91. With respect to enhanced credit, the
courts seem to require some evidence, although the manner in which that
evidence or information is presented varies considerably.  In the case of
R
.
v.
Joseph
,
2012 BCCA 359 (CanLII)
,
2012 BCCA 359 (QL), the issue of the nature of the evidentiary burden imposed
by s. 719(3.1) of the
Code
was addressed, albeit in
obiter
.
As Harris J.A. explained (at paras. 31-33):

The
Truth
in Sentencing Act
does not explicitly amend the traditional sentencing
procedure. There is nothing in s. 719 that amends the procedure by
implication. There is no reason in principle to depart from the general rules
applicable to all sentencing hearings when a court is asked to decide whether
the circumstances justify granting enhanced credit.

Sections
723 and 724 of the
Code
make it clear that a court may rely on
submissions, hearsay and agreed facts in sentencing.
R.
v.
Gardiner
,

1982 CanLII 30 (SCC)
, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 368,
68 C.C.C. (2d) 477, confirms that strict evidentiary rules do not apply unless
matters are contested. ….

In my
view, the same general principles that govern providing the court with the
necessary facts or information for the purpose of sentencing apply to
s. 719(3.1).

92. Thus, there are cases where the evidence
was presented through
viva voce
testimony by the accused and prison officials,
through affidavits or agreed statements of fact, or simply presented as part of
counsel’s submissions.

[…]

94. The bottom line is, as Green J. noted in
Johnson
(at para. 189):

…. Further,
and here adapting the words of Cole J. in
R
. v.
Duff
,
2010 ONCJ 493 (CanLII)
, [2010 ONCJ 493 (QL)],
before acting on such claim [of arduous or oppressive remand conditions] “
a
sentencing judge should have some evidence that the ... [remand] conditions ...
have been particularly onerous
”. This may not prove an arduous evidentiary
burden, but it is one that need be met where the exercise of judicial
discretion replaces the application of settled formulae.

(emphasis added)

[
105
]

In the present case, the defense provided no
evidence whatsoever that Mr. Anderson’s remand conditions were
particularly onerous. On the contrary, other than citing the
Carvery

decision (referred to by Justice Steel in
Stonefish
), M
e
Kennedy
presented nothing which would justify a derogation from the ratio of 1:1 set
out at section 718 (3) Cr. C.
[17]
.

[
106
]

In accordance with sections 719 (3) and
719 (3.2) Cr. C., the Court will therefore impose a 1:1 ratio, given
that the defense failed to meet its burden to furnish evidence which would
justify a derogation from that ratio in accordance with article
719 (3.1) Cr. C.

[
107
]

In conclusion then and taking into account all
of the foregoing facts and circumstances, as well as the principles outlined in
sections 718 and following of the
Criminal Code
, the Court will impose the
following sentence.

[
108
]

On the count of robbery at the Laurentian Bank
on March 17
th
, 2010, Barrington Anderson will be sentenced to five
years in prison, and on the count of use of an imitation weapon in the
commission of the indictable offence of robbery, also on March 17
th
,
2010, Mr. Anderson will be sentenced to one year in prison, to be served
consecutively to the sentence on the count of robbery.

[
109
]

Furthermore, the Court will impose the ratio of
one day for each day of pre-trial detention, for the reasons given above.

[
110
]

As a result, Barrington Anderson will be
sentenced to a global sentence of six years incarceration, to be served
from the date of his arrest on August 30
th
, 2010. As a result, he
will serve an additional 42 months (3.5 years) from the present date.

[
111
]

In virtue of section
109 (3) Cr. C, the Court will prohibit Mr. Anderson from
possessing any firearm, cross-bow, prohibited weapon, restricted weapon,
prohibited device, ammunition, prohibited ammunition and explosive substance
and this, for life, given the circumstances of the commission of these offences
and given his previous convictions.

[
112
]

The Court will also make an order that a number
of samples of bodily substances be taken for forensic DNA purposes, pursuant to
section 487.051 Cr. C., given not only the circumstances of the
commission of these offences, in particular the offence of robbery, but also
Mr. Anderson’s previous criminal record.

[
113
]

For all of the foregoing reasons:

BARRINGTON
ANDERSON, THE COURT IMPOSES THE FOLLOWING SENTENCE ON YOU:

[
114
]

On the count of robbery at the Laurentian Bank
on March 17
th
, 2010, the Court sentences you, Barrington Anderson,
to a term of imprisonment in a penitentiary of five years;

[
115
]

On the count of use of an imitation weapon in
the commission of the indictable offence of robbery on March 17
th
,
2010, the Court sentences you, Barrington Anderson to a term of imprisonment in
a penitentiary of one year, to be served consecutively to the sentence of five
years on the count of robbery, for a total sentence of six years.

[
116
]

Given the provisions of
section 719 (3.1)
of the

Criminal Code
, the Court will take into account 2.5 years of preventative
detention on the ratio of one day for each day of such pre-trial detention.

[
117
]

Therefore, Barrington Anderson, you are
sentenced to a global sentence of six years incarceration, to be calculated
from the date of your arrest on August 30
th
, 2010, and therefore,
for an additional period of three and one half years, or 42 months, from
today’s date.

[
118
]

In virtue of
section 109(3)
of the
Criminal
Code
, the Court prohibits you, Barrington Anderson, from possessing any
firearm, cross-bow, prohibited weapon, restricted weapon, prohibited device,
ammunition, prohibited ammunition and explosive substance, for life.

[
119
]

The Court will make an order that a number of
samples of bodily substances be taken for forensic DNA purposes, pursuant to

section 487.051
of the

.
